changed_views: Agent distribution is tied to product accessibility: exposing pricing and completing administrative APIs can matter alongside recommendation tracking. The episode offers mechanisms and anecdotes, not an attribution study.

Resend’s described position is expanding from developer experience into owned mail transport and persistent agent inboxes; the October launch posts confirm those moves were public before this episode was published.
MCP call volume and npm downloads reveal usage of particular interfaces. They should not be substituted for active-customer growth, email-volume share or company revenue.
follow_ups: Look for unique active MCP accounts, task success, retention and paid conversion by interface, rather than extrapolating from tool-call totals.
Test the Markdown-pricing mechanism with a stable query set and named model versions; distinguish answer accuracy from referral or revenue uplift.
Track Forge adoption, delivery latency, provider acceptance versus inbox placement, and cost per delivered message as migration expands.
Watch Inboxes usage and enterprise expansion with named customer outcomes; separate launch availability from durable commercial traction.

signals.claim: Rocha says Resend’s MCP usage reached roughly 1.2 million calls in August, while building a remote service required revisiting OAuth, roles and resource permissions rather than merely wrapping the send-email API.
signals.evidence: He describes recent monthly doubling and faster growth than the CLI, without supplying unique-user, retention or revenue figures. The MCP expanded from roughly 20 tools to more than 80 at recording. He identifies response size and coverage of billing, team invitations, provisioning and deletion as difficult design questions; a larger tool count is not a demonstrated success-rate improvement. The [current official MCP documentation](https://resend.com/docs/mcp-server) corroborates hosted OAuth and broad management capabilities. Separately, the [September 22 headless-dashboard initiative](https://resend.com/blog/headless-dashboard-initiative) describes programmatic coverage as ongoing work. Rocha remains undecided about unauthenticated provisioning because of abuse risk.

signals.claim: Rocha’s clearest AEO example is correcting an agent’s pricing calculation by exposing the underlying numbers as Markdown. It demonstrates a practical information-access problem, without establishing which tactics cause more recommendations or sales.
signals.evidence: An agent incorrectly compared the cost of sending 1.2 million emails because the relevant prices sat behind an interactive widget. Rocha says he added a Markdown pricing representation and got a correct answer when he tried again days later. He also describes FAQ pages, framework-specific guides, llms.txt and text equivalents of chart data. The [live pricing.md page](https://resend.com/pricing.md) contains tiers, allowances and overages, confirming the implementation exists. The before-and-after anecdote lacks a fixed model, query set or control group. Swyx’s separate story of an agent selecting Resend despite an existing provider illustrates delegated vendor selection, not measured category dominance.

signals.claim: Rocha describes Resend moving from a developer-facing layer on Amazon SES toward owning the sending infrastructure, seeking tighter control over throughput, latency and observability.
signals.evidence: He says the original strategy focused on SDKs and developer experience while SES supplied delivery. Operating the surrounding events, logs and queues added complexity. The next phase involves owned IP blocks, provider-specific traffic control and direct mailbox-provider relationships; he also says the sending path moved from JavaScript to Go. The interview frames the infrastructure announcement as forthcoming. A separate [October 23 Forge announcement](https://resend.com/blog/announcing-resend-forge) confirms Resend announced its own mail transfer agent and customer activation. That corroborates the direction, but neither the interview nor this check establishes margin improvement or independently measured inbox placement.

signals.claim: Rocha describes agent inboxes as a higher-level product than inbound-email webhooks: provision addresses and expose persistent mailbox operations that agents can share with people.
signals.evidence: He discusses creating many inboxes programmatically, then providing operations such as read state, starring and labels, with a shared-inbox experience as the comparison. This is a roadmap discussion at recording, not a claim that basic inbound webhooks already deliver a complete agent mailbox. The separate [October 22 Inboxes launch](https://resend.com/blog/announcing-inboxes) confirms an API-first product with threaded conversations, team collaboration and agent access through API, CLI and MCP. The announcement establishes release, not customer adoption, reliability or revenue from this new surface.

signals.claim: Rocha reports 4.3 million users and more than 120,000 paid customers while Resend is only beginning its enterprise sales motion. He explicitly distinguishes SDK-download momentum from the incumbent’s much larger email volume.
signals.evidence: The user and paid-customer counts are recording-time company claims with no activity window or cohort definitions, so they do not support a paid-conversion calculation. Rocha says Resend’s npm SDK downloads exceeded twice SendGrid’s, then acknowledges SendGrid still sends substantially more email. He reports one account executive and argues that enterprise needs a different product, beyond adding SSO and audit logs. No attributable revenue increase from that salesperson is disclosed. The later $10 million versus $100 million ARR discussion is explicitly a hypothetical family-priority scenario ten years ahead, not current revenue guidance.

summary: Zeno Rocha explains how Resend is adapting an email infrastructure business to agents as both users and distribution channels. The useful evidence concerns rising MCP activity, the permissions and API work behind a headless product, machine-readable pricing, and expansion into owned sending infrastructure and agent inboxes. Commercial counts are company-reported snapshots, not revenue or market-share measures. Published November 10, the interview refers to August activity and the day of an Astra launch without establishing an exact recording date; product announcements checked separately show that two discussed roadmap items launched in October. Host swyx discloses that he is an investor in Resend.
why_it_matters: Agent access is becoming part of the product itself: authentication, account operations, readable commercial information and persistent inbox state all affect whether an agent can discover and use a service. Resend also illustrates a developer-experience business moving into infrastructure ownership. The interview provides concrete implementation choices and adoption claims, while leaving the economics and causal impact of its distribution tactics unmeasured.
